newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Massacre prompted Australian gun law reform.
newsitem.headline: Massacre prompted Australian gun law reform.

text.p: Rampaging gunman Martin Bryant achieved with a semi-automatic rifle in just a few hours last April what Australia's frustrated anti-gun lobby had failed to do in years of campaigning for stricter gun controls.
The Port Arthur massacre, in which 35 people died, shocked the country. What couldn't happen in Australia, had happened.
Campaigners who had often previously looked to other countries for shocking examples of gun violence now had to look no further than the normally tranquil island state of Tasmania.
"We may never know why Martin Bryant massacred 35 men, women and children at Port Arthur on that terrible Sunday last April," Melbourne's The Age newspaper said in an editorial this week.

"But we know how he did it, and that is something we must never forget ... Port Arthur will now be remembered for the infamy of Martin Bryant and -- we hope -- for a sea change in Australian attitudes to gun ownership and control."
On Friday a court in Tasmania sentenced Bryant to life imprisonment without parole.
Survivors of the massacre reacted with mixed emotions to Bryant's life sentence, but all agreed the strict gun laws his murderous rampage created should now be enforced.

"I urge Australians to be vigilant in line with gun law reforms and we owe this to the 35 people who so cruelly lost their lives at Port Arthur," said Walter Mikac, whose wife and two infant daughters were mercilessly gunned down.
"Our debt to them is to make Australia a safe place to be."
Australia's federal and state governments have already moved to prevent a recurrence, despite mass demonstrations around the country by angry gun owners in recent months.
But opinion polls showed up to 90 percent acceptance for a crackdown on firearms.
Within weeks of the massacre, Australia's most conservative state governments had accepted the need for restrictions they had formerly refused to countenance.

In July, Australia's states agreed to Canberra's demand to ban self-loading guns, with few exceptions. Conservative states failed in a last-ditch attempt to save pump-action shotguns if their magazines were restricted to just two shells.
Prime Minister John Howard said this process, known as crimping, could be reversed and threatened the states and pro-gun lobby with a national referendum on the issue.
With Australia's urban population now overwhelmingly hostile to almost any guns, the conservative states had no choice but to agree.
The bans were unpopular in rural areas, although a supposed political backlash against Howard has failed to emerge in opinion polls.
The results were a national ban on almost all self-loading guns and a government buy-back of banned weapons that will cost the average taxpayer Australian A$70 (US$57).
The funds will be raised by a one-off increase in the national health insurance levy to 1.7 percent from 1.5 percent, raising about A$500 million in the year to June 1997.
About 170,000 guns have already been passed in at a cost of about A$75 million.
There are an estimated four million privately owned firearms in Australia, a nation of 18 million.
But pro-gun activists say many guns will simply be hidden.
"We are urging gun owners to bury early and bury often," Firearm Owners Association Vice President Ian McNiven told reporters in July.

The Tasmanian Supreme Court heard this week how Bryant bought several high-powered, semi-automatic rifles and thousands of rounds of military-style ammunition in the months leading up to the massacre, despite not having a firearms licence.
